sec.title: Background
sec.p: Based on the landmark PLATO (Platelet Inhibition and Patient Outcomes) and TRITON‐TIMI 38 (Trial to Assess Improvement in Therapeutic Outcomes by Optimizing Platelet Inhibition With Prasugrel–Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction) trials, current guidelines recommend ticagrelor and prasugrel over clopidogrel for acute coronary syndrome. However, subsequent studies have failed to replicate the reported benefits of ticagrelor, raising concerns about the validity of the PLATO trial's findings.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Randomized trials published until January 2025 were searched on PubMed and Embase and included if they compared 2 of the 3 standard dual antiplatelet therapies: 12 months aspirin plus clopidogrel, prasugrel, or ticagrelor. We constructed a network with and without PLATO to assess its impact on the synthesized risk estimates on major adverse cardiovascular events, patient mortality, myocardial infarction, and stent thrombosis, as well as major bleeding and major or minor bleeding.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Twelve trials, enrolling 52 415 patients (clopidogrel: 23 557; ticagrelor: 13 344, prasugrel: 15 514) were included. The analysis with PLATO showed lower hazard ratios for ticagrelor versus clopidogrel than the analysis without PLATO in major adverse cardiovascular events, mortality, myocardial infarction, and bleeding outcomes (e.g., cardiovascular mortality; hazard ratio [HR], 0.83 [95% CI, 0.72–0.96] when PLATO was included; HR, 0.96 [95% CI, 0.73–1.25] when PLATO was excluded). Ticagrelor and prasugrel were associated with higher incidences of major bleeding and major or minor bleeding for analyses including and excluding PLATO, altohugh the point estimates for ticagrelor were lower when PLATO was included.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The pooled estimates with PLATO favored ticagrelor compared with estimates without PLATO in several studied outcomes, potentially suggesting the substantial impacts of PLATO's findings on the pooled risk estimates; therefore, additional evidence may be needed given the large number of patients worldwide treated with dual antiplatelet therapy.
Keywords: acute coronary syndrome, clinical trial, dual antiplatelet therapy, guideline

Trial to Assess Improvement in Therapeutic Outcomes by Optimizing Platelet Inhibition With Prasugrel–Thrombolysis In Myocardial Infarction

list-item.p: This study synthesized the previous clinical trials comparing clopidogrel‐, ticagrelor‐, and prasugrel‐based 12‐month dual antiplatelet therapy for acute coronary sydnrome by network meta‐analysis, both with and without the inclusion of the PLATO (Platelet Inhibition and Patient Outcomes) trial, and examined the impacts of PLATO on the pooled estimates.

Out of the assessed outcomes, the risk estimates for ticagrelor compared with clopidogrel or prasugrel in major adverse cardiovascular events, all‐cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, myocardial infarction, major bleeding, and major or minor bleeding, were lower when the PLATO trial was included, potentially suggesting the substantial impacts of PLATO on the pooled risk estimates.

Current guidelines' recommendations for ticagrelor based on a single clinical trial, the results of which are inconsistent with those of other studies, may benefit from further reevaluation and additional data.

body.p: The key components of treatment for acute coronary syndrome (ACS) entail early reperfusion and antithrombotic therapies. 1 , 2 Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin and P2Y12 inhibitors has been shown to reduce major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with ACS and is recommended to continue for 12 months as the default in clinical guidelines. 1 , 2 In particular, ticagrelor and prasugrel are preferred over clopidogrel unless they are unavailable or contraindicated because of their faster onset of action and more potent nature of platelet inhibition. This preference is explicitly stated as a class 1 recommendation in both European and American guidelines, primarily based on the results from the PLATO (Platelet Inhibition and Patient Outcomes) and TRITON‐TIMI 38 (Trial to Assess Improvement in Therapeutic Outcomes by Optimizing Platelet Inhibition With Prasugrel–Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction) trials. 1 , 2 , 3 , 4

However, concerns have been raised about the validity of the findings of the PLATO trial. 5 , 6 The PLATO trial showed the superiority of ticagrelor to clopidogrel with or without early revascularization and facilitated the expansion of ticagrelor with broad indications internationally. 3 , 6 Meanwhile, there have been criticisms about the unexplained geographical variation observed in this trial. Specifically, the superiority of ticagrelor was confined to sponsor‐monitored sites. Subgroup analyses of the United States (where all sites were monitored independently by third‐party clinical research organizations) showed a hazard ratio (HR) for MACE of 1.27 (95% CI, 0.92–1.75), as opposed to an HR of 0.81 (95% CI, 0.74–0.90) outside the United States. Furthermore, subsequent studies failed to replicate the superiority of ticagrelor over clopidogrel. 7 , 8 There have also been allegations of bias arising from the end point adjudication process. For example, the case number of myocardial infarction (MI) increased by 45, only in the clopidogrel group, after an adjudication process. Furthermore, the accuracy of death records has been questioned. Some of the death records submitted to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) reportedly did not match the original trial documents shared by some sites. Moreover, the 45 deaths that occurred during the follow‐up period were omitted from the original publication as deaths after consent withdrawal, favoring ticagrelor. 5

Because the results from this landmark trial have had major impacts on the recommendations of international guidelines, the number of individuals affected by this trial and the costs associated with its prescription are tremendous. For instance, the annual incidence of ACS in the United States is estimated to be 805 000, and the US government spent >$750 million in 2022 for ticagrelor. 5 , 9 Therefore, in the present study, we conducted a network meta‐analysis of randomized clinical trials comparing P2Y12 inhibitors, with and without inclusion of the results from the PLATO trial, to evaluate the impacts of this trial on the pooled direct and indirect estimates and to reassess the appropriateness of the current recommendations.

sec.title: METHODS
sec.p: This research was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses reporting guidelines and registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD42025632269). 10 No patients were directly involved, because the present study was a trial‐level meta‐analysis, and no primary data were collected. No patients were asked to advise on the interpretation or authoring of the article. Ethics exemption/institutional review board approval was granted. Patient consent was not required for the study. No funding sources were involved in determining the study design; in the collection, analysis, and interpretation of data; in the writing of the report; and in the decision to submit the article for publication. The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

sec.title: Data Source and Search Strategy
sec.p: Two independent investigators (A.W. and T.K.) conducted a comprehensive literature search on PubMed and Embase on January 7, 2025, and individually screened the eligibility of each study. After screening the articles based on title and abstract, the full texts of potentially eligible studies were collected for further review. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion. The search terms are summarized in Tables S1 and S2.

sec.title: Eligibility Criteria
sec.p: Studies were included if they were (1) published in a peer‐reviewed journal, (2) randomized clinical trials, (3) enrolled patients with ACS, (4) compared 2 of the 3 DAPT strategies (ie, 12 months of aspirin plus [clopidogrel, prasugrel, or ticagrelor]), and (5) included follow‐up periods of at least 12 months. Trials comparing different durations of DAPT strategies were not included, because the focus of this study was to evaluate different P2Y12 inhibitors that aligned with current guideline recommendations of 12‐month DAPT after ACS. The risk of bias in each trial was assessed using the Cochrane Collaboration risk of bias 2.0 tool.

sec.title: Data Items
sec.p: The baseline characteristics of each trial, such as the first author or the trial name, publication year, sponsorship, sample size, and compared drugs, were tabulated.

Next, the following efficacy outcome data were extracted: MACE, all‐cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, MI, stroke, and stent thrombosis. For safety outcomes, major bleeding and combined major or minor bleeding were extracted. We collected the data according to each trial's prespecified definition for each outcome.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: A network of the included trials was constructed with and without inclusion of the PLATO trial to assess the impact of PLATO on the pooled estimates for each outcome using the frequentist approach. HRs and 95% CIs for each outcome were synthesized by a random‐effects model for each pair of treatments, assuming a common heterogeneity variance across all treatment comparisons. If the HR was unavailable, the risk ratio at the 12‐month follow‐up was used as a substitute, because the risk ratio can approximate the HR when the incidence during the follow‐up is ≈≤10%. 11 , 12 The Q statistic and I 2 were used to qualitatively and quantitatively assess the heterogeneity of each outcome across the trials. The Q statistic is calculated as the weighted sum of squared differences between the pooled effects and individual study's effect, and its P values can inform the presence of heterogeneity. I 2 quantifies the degree of heterogeneity using the Q statistic in relation to the number of studies. In network meta‐analyses, both measures can be used to assess the heterogeneity of direct and indirect estimates; heterogeneity refers to variation across studies within the same designs, whereas inconsistency refers to variation between different designs. 13 To establish a hierarchy of the competing therapies for each outcome, we summarized the relative ranking of each treatment using P scores. P scores are a frequentist metric, expressed on a scale from 0 to 1, with a higher P score indicating a higher certainty that a treatment is superior to other treatments in the network; a score of 1 suggests the treatment is certain to be the best option, whereas a score of 0 suggests it is certain to be the worst. Publication bias was assessed by the funnel plot and Egger test. 14

Several sensitivity analyses were also performed. First, we pooled the risk ratio (calculated based on the event numbers at the 12‐month follow‐up) instead of the HR for all included trials to avoid the inconsistency arising from different effect measures. Second, we restricted the patients to those undergoing percutaneous coronary interventions (PCI). Only trials designed to provide all patients with early revascularization or trials with subgroup analysis according to PCI were used for this analysis. Third, patients' age was restricted to ≤75 years, because current guidelines recommend ticagrelor/prasugrel over clopidogrel, particularly among the younger population (this analysis was conducted only for MACE, given the limited number of studies reporting the results according to the participants' age). 1 , 15 Fourth, to address the possibility that the heterogeneity in the risk estimates was attributable to regional differences, we performed a subgroup analysis for MACE according to regions. Due to the limited number of trials reporting the results by regions, we only assessed the Asia‐Pacific region and Europe. Fifth, industry‐sponsored trials were excluded to explore other sources of heterogeneity.

sec.title: Study Characteristics
sec.p: In total, we constructed a network of 12 randomized trials, with 5 trials comparing ticagrelor with clopidogrel, 3 , 7 , 8 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 5 trials comparing prasugrel with clopidogrel, 4 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 and 2 trials comparing ticagrelor with prasugrel (Figure S1). 24 , 25 These studies collectively enrolled 52 415 patients (ticagrelor: 13 344, prasugrel: 15 514, clopidogrel: 23 557) (Figure 1); the reasons for the exclusion of each study after full‐text review are summarized in Table S3. Seven trials were industry‐sponsored (TableTable). Based on the risk of bias tool, all trials were considered to have a low risk of bias (Table S4).

sec.title: Main Analysis
sec.p: The definitions of outcomes and the effect estimates for each trial are summarized in Tables S5 and S6. For the assessment of publication bias, funnel plots were more symmetric when the PLATO trial was excluded than when it was included for the end points of MACE, all‐cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, MI, and major or minor bleeding (Figures S2–S9).

sec.title: Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events
sec.p: Risk estimates including PLATO did not find differences in MACE between patients receiving ticagrelor versus prasugrel (HR, 1.01 [95% CI, 0.84–1.21]) or patients receiving prasugrel versus clopidogrel (HR, 0.90 [95% CI, 0.78–1.04]). In the estimates without PLATO, which showed less pronounced heterogeneity (I 2, 55.8% versus 62.3%) and inconsistency (I 2, 0% versus 73.8%) than estimates with PLATO, there was similarly no evidence that ticagrelor or prasugrel was associated with a lower risk of MACE (ticagrelor versus clopidogrel: HR, 1.12 [95% CI, 0.91–1.37]; prasugrel versus clopidogrel: HR, 0.91 [95% CI, 0.80–1.04]; Figure 2 and Table S7), although the point estimate for ticagrelor was higher when PLATO was excluded. The relative ranking by P scores is summarized in Table S8.

sec.title: Mortality
sec.p: Ticagrelor or prasugrel was not associated with all‐cause mortality, compared with clopidogrel, in the network estimates with or without the PLATO trial, with the analyses including PLATO being more heterogeneous and inconsistent (Figure 2; Table S7). The lower HR for ticagrelor compared with clopidogrel in all‐cause mortality was reversed when PLATO was excluded (Figure 2; Table S8). Similarly, although ticagrelor was associated with lower cardiovascular mortality than clopidogrel (HR, 0.83 [95% CI, 0.72–0.96]) in analyses with PLATO (Figure 2), the point estimate was closer to 1 when PLATO was excluded (HR, 0.96 [95% CI, 0.73–1.25]).

sec.title: MI, Stroke, and Stent Thrombosis
sec.p: For MI, risk estimates with PLATO showed between‐designs inconsistency (Q statistic, 3.92 [P=0.048]; I 2, 74.5%), whereas estimates without PLATO did not (Q statistic, 0.30 [P=0.581]; I 2, 0%) (Table S7). The point estimate for ticagrelor compared with clopidogrel was reversed between estimates with versus without the data from the PLATO trial (Figure 2).

The risk estimates for stroke were similar between the analysis with and without PLATO (Figure 2). Meanwhile, both ticagrelor and prasugrel were associated with lower incidences of stent thrombosis in analyses with PLATO (ticagrelor versus clopidogrel: HR, 0.72 [95% CI, 0.58–0.89]; prasugrel versus clopidogrel: HR, 0.49 [95% CI, 0.39–0.63]) and without PLATO (ticagrelor versus clopidogrel: HR, 0.58 [95% CI, 0.34–0.99]; prasugrel versus clopidogrel: HR, 0.47 [95% CI, 0.36–0.62]). There was no evidence of heterogeneity or inconsistency in the estimates with and without PLATO for stent thrombosis (Table S7).

sec.title: Safety Outcomes
sec.p: Both ticagrelor and prasugrel were associated with higher incidences of major bleeding in analyses with PLATO (ticagrelor versus clopidogrel: HR, 1.19 [95% CI, 1.02–1.39]; prasugrel versus clopidogrel: HR, 1.20 [95% CI, 0.99–1.45]) and without PLATO (ticagrelor versus clopidogrel: HR, 1.43 [95% CI, 1.16–1.77]; prasugrel versus clopidogrel: HR, 1.28 [95% CI, 1.08–1.52]), with the point estimate for ticagrelor versus clopidogrel being higher when PLATO was excluded. Both ticagrelor and prasugrel were associated with higher incidences of major or minor bleeding in analyses with or without PLATO, with ticagrelor having the lowest P scores (Figure 3; Table S8).

sec.title: Sensitivity Analyses
sec.p: The findings were qualitatively unaffected by pooling risk ratio instead of HR (Table S9), restricting the patients to PCI subgroup (Table S10), restricting patients to those aged ≤75 years (Table S11), and separately analyzing different regions (Table S12). The point estimates of ticagrelor compared with clopidogrel for MACE, all‐cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, MI, and bleeding outcomes were higher when PLATO was not included. Additionally, in the PCI subgroup, prasugrel was associated with lower incidences of MACE (HR, 0.75 [95% CI, 0.59–0.95]) and MI (HR, 0.64 [95% CI, 0.50–0.83]) than ticagrelor in analyses without PLATO. When only non‐industry‐sponsored trials were included (Table S13), the risks of MACE was similar among patients receiving clopidogrel, ticagrelor, and prasugrel, whereas ticagrelor was associated with higher incidences of major bleeding and major or minor bleeding compared with clopidogrel.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: In this network meta‐analysis comparing the 3 current standard DAPT strategies for patients with ACS, we found that the inclusion of the PLATO trial significantly influenced the pooled risk estimates and contributed to the inconsistencies in some of the outcomes. For example, all‐cause and cardiovascular mortality differed in analyses with and without the PLATO trial. Our findings will offer an opportunity to reassess the appropriateness of the current recommendations.

sec.title: Concerns Raised About the Integrity of the Trial
sec.p: The PLATO trial, published in 2009, was one of the largest randomized trials in cardiovascular medicine and demonstrated that ticagrelor reduced mortality compared with clopidogrel in patients with ACS by 22%, which was striking for many clinicians at the time. These results, alongside the TRITON‐TIMI 38 trial, which showed the superiority of prasugrel over clopidogrel in reducing MACE for patients with ACS, led to the belief that both ticagrelor and prasugrel were superior to clopidogrel. Consequently, these drugs received a strong recommendation in clinical guidelines. 1 , 2 Because this preference for ticagrelor/prasugrel over clopidogrel was based on these landmark trials, the validity of these trials is critical. Some of the FDA reviewers raised concerns about the PLATO trial's findings during the approval process. 26 For example, patients in the ticagrelor group experienced higher incidences of non‐MI thrombotic events, such as peripheral ischemia, pulmonary embolism, renal ischemia, and retinal ischemia, 26 compared with clopidogrel, which is not consistent with the observed 16% reduction in MI. Moreover, data were initially presented to the FDA with complete follow‐up for all except for 5 patients; however, subsequently, it was revealed that 531 patients did not have vital status follow‐up at the end of the study, raising concerns about the trial's completeness and accuracy. 26 , 27 More problematically, a greater proportion of patients in the ticagrelor group had incomplete vital status follow‐up (3.1% versus 2.6%), which could potentially negate the significant mortality reduction observed with the use of ticagrelor.

sec.title: Unproven Accusations
sec.p: Amid these concerns, the US Department of Justice sought the documents and information related to the PLATO trial from the sponsor but ultimately closed the investigation in 2014. 28 At the time, the FDA division director expressed their opinions that the data quality issues were few and of no great concern, 29 stating that “missed events would have had to have been very skewed from the overall study to have impacted the outcome.” 26 One notable issue raised during the approval process was the geographical variation in the efficacy of ticagrelor. In response, the sponsor proposed the aspirin hypothesis, suggesting that the combination of ticagrelor and high‐dose aspirin contributed to higher incidences of thrombotic events. 30 This hypothesis was supported by the observation that approximately 50% of patients in the United States received ≥300 mg of maintenance aspirin, as opposed to only 2% of patients outside the United States. 26 , 30 In exploratory analyses conducted by senior statisticians, the aspirin dose played the most significant role in changing the interaction coefficient in their statistical models. 30 , 31 However, the exact reason why the combination of high‐dose aspirin and ticagrelor may increase thrombotic events remains uncertain. Although there is a possibility that the higher aspirin doses could have prothrombotic effects rather than antithrombotic effects in the presence of strong P2Y12 inhibition, 30 , 32 such a phenomenon has not been clinically proven. 33 Of note, the independent analyses of an FDA medical officer did not confirm a significant interaction between ticagrelor and high‐dose aspirin. 26 , 34

sec.title: Interpreting the Results of the Current Study
sec.p: Our findings should be interpreted in this context. In our network meta‐analysis, inconsistencies between designs were more prevalent in the analysis including PLATO, potentially suggesting that the results from PLATO could be outliers. It is notable that, by solely excluding the PLATO trial, the P score of ticagrelor for all‐cause mortality shifted from the highest to the lowest, and the significant difference in cardiovascular mortality between ticagrelor and clopidogrel became almost negligible, meaning that the mortality benefits of ticagrelor were solely derived from the PLATO trial. The present study also aligned with the ISAR‐REACT 5 (Intracoronary Stenting and Antithrombotic Regimen: Rapid Early Action for Coronary Treatment 5) trial, a non‐industry‐sponsored head‐to‐head comparison of ticagrelor versus prasugrel in patients undergoing early revascularization. 24 In the ISAR‐REACT 5 trial, ticagrelor was associated with higher incidences of MACE and MI with HRs of 1.36 and 1.63, respectively, which were fairly similar to our sensitivity analysis excluding PLATO among patients undergoing PCI.

Our results provide further implications for contemporary strategies stemming from the PLATO trial. Although DAPT is recommended to continue for 12 months after ACS as a default, 1 , 2 shorter duration (1–6 months) of DAPT followed by ticagrelor monotherapy is also recommended as class 1 as a bleeding reduction strategy in the latest American guidelines, 2 given the similar effectiveness in preventing thrombotic events and a lower risk of bleeding events compared with the 12‐month ticagrelor‐based DAPT strategy. 2 , 35 , 36 , 37 , 38 , 39 However, it is important to recognize that previous clinical trials evaluating different durations of DAPT have used the same P2Y12 inhibitors in both the intervention and control arms (ie, ticagrelor‐based short DAPT followed by ticagrelor monotherapy versus ticagrelor‐based 12‐month DAPT, rather than ticagrelor‐based short DAPT followed by ticagrelor monotherapy versus clopidogrel‐based 12‐month DAPT). 35 , 36 , 40 , 41 , 42 In other words, these trials have compared the efficacy and safety of the shorter DAPT followed by ticagrelor monotherapy with the “standard” 12‐month ticagrelor plus aspirin, 35 , 36 , 40 on the premise that 12‐month ticagrelor plus aspirin is superior to 12‐month clopidogrel plus aspirin. Therefore, the validity of the data on 12‐month DAPT strategies, such as those derived from the PLATO trial, is crucial when interpreting the emerging evidence on shorter DAPT regimens.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: The present study had limitations. First, this was a network meta‐analysis of trial‐level data and was unable to provide granular information on specific populations, such as patients with high bleeding risk or underrepresented populations. 1 , 15 Second, although we attempted to explore clinically relevant effect‐modifying variables including age, other factors may also be related to the differences between P2Y12 inhibitors, such as underlying comorbidities and concurrent treatments. 26 Third, because the included studies were published from 2007 to 2020, during which time drug‐eluting stents for PCI also evolved, 43 the findings of our study may not necessarily reflect contemporary practice. However, because newer generations of drug‐eluting stents are less likely to cause thrombotic events, 44 the clinically meaningful differences between prasugrel/ticagrelor and clopidogrel may not be of major concern. This shift could reduce the relative benefit of prasugrel and ticagrelor over clopidogrel in the context of modern stent technology.

sec.title: CONCLUSIONS
sec.p: This network meta‐analysis compared the current standard 12‐month DAPT strategies with different P2Y12 inhibitors and revealed inconsistent results with versus without including the results from the PLATO trial. Regardless of whether the concerns about the PLATO trial's integrity were true, the substantial impacts of this single trial on the pooled estimates were noteworthy. Given the widespread use of DAPT and its significant financial implications, the current recommendations reliant on a single trial may benefit from additional data.
